OceanTraX — measuring the ocean's temperature from Ships of Opportunity

The OceanTraX Network

The upper ocean — the top 1,000 metres — stores more than 90% of the excess heat being accumulated by Earth's climate system. How that heat is distributed, transported, and exchanged with the atmosphere is one of the most important questions in climate science. It shapes ENSO forecasts, drives regional climate patterns, and is a key indicator of long-term global warming. But measuring it across the vastness of the world's ocean basins is a formidable challenge.

Since 1980, the OceanTraX network has been meeting that challenge by deploying oceanographic instruments from commercial vessels on regular trade routes. Rather than requiring dedicated research ships — expensive and limited in number — OceanTrax puts measurement systems onto vessels that are already crossing the ocean for other purposes. The result is a cost-effective, globally distributed network of ocean thermal observations that complements the Argo float network and satellite altimetry but cannot be repolaced by them.

What OceanTraX measures — the instruments

~60

active OceanTraX ships

~19,000

XBTs deployed annually

36

repeat XBT lines

The primary instrument of OceanTraX is the eXpendable BathyThermograph (XBT) — a compact temperature probe that is deployed from the ship’s deck at prescribed intervals along the route. As the probe falls through the water column, a computer records the temperature vs. depth continuously from the surface down to typically about 850m deep.When the probe’s thin wire is depleted, and the probe it sinks to the sea floor, no recovery is required.

XBT data are automatically quality-controlled and transmitted in real time via satellite to data centres worldwide within 24 hours. In a typical year, approximately 50% of XBT deployments occur in the Pacific Ocean, 35% in the Atlantic, and 15% in the Indian Ocean. About twenty agencies are currently involved in OceanTrax operations.

Beyond XBTs, OceanTrax also coordinates with other networks that use ships of opportunity as platforms for gathering atmoshperhic and physical oceanographic data to help recruit and deploy their instrumentation on these shared volunteer ships.
